null.method: shuffled copies of this window with the repeat mask and every dinucleotide count kept, scanned and collapsed the same way

scan_quality.fdp_note: about 45% of these 17 sites (range 24% to 65%) would be expected on shuffled sequence of this window, so roughly 9 are above chance; among the best-scoring sites the share is lower: 31% of the top 5, 39% of the top 10. Estimated from 30 shuffled copies that keep the repeat mask and every dinucleotide count. The formula that assumes each motif matches at exactly its stated p-value would expect 9 and is not used. Nothing here says which sites are real; only ChIP evidence separates them.

occupancy.note: 10 of 17 factors have a measured peak over this window and 7 do not. A shuffled copy of the window cannot produce a peak, so the share of this scan the null expects by chance - about 8 of its 17 factors - is attributed to those 7: about 100% of them are consistent with chance, against roughly 7% of the measured ones. This matters for the ranking because NR1H4 has a ligand and no measured occupancy: every drug reaching the gene through it rests on a predicted site. RXRA has both a ligand and a measured peak, which is the stronger footing. A peak says something bound here in the cell type the atlas used. It does not say this factor is what bound, and it is not a measurement in your cells.

routes.what_it_does: redirects splicing so a productive transcript is made — exon inclusion, exon skipping, or suppression of a cryptic site
drugs: Risdiplam (FDA-approved, SMA — small molecule, oral)
Nusinersen (FDA-approved, SMA — intrathecal ASO)
Eteplirsen, golodirsen, viltolarsen, casimersen (FDA accelerated approval, DMD exon skipping)
Branaplam (clinical; SMN2 splice modifier)
routes.applies_when: a splice-site or splice-regulatory variant, a poison exon, or a paralog whose splicing can be redirected (SMN2)
caveats: Exon-skipping restores a partly functional, internally deleted protein, not a wild-type one — the DMD agents are judged on dystrophin that is shorter than normal.
Accelerated approvals in this class rest on a surrogate endpoint (protein level), and the confirmatory functional benefit has been contested.
Small-molecule splice modifiers are not fully gene-specific; risdiplam alters splicing of other transcripts too.

routes.what_it_does: lengthens mRNA half-life, usually through AU-rich elements in the 3'UTR and the proteins that bind them. Doubling half-life doubles steady-state message with no change in transcription
drugs: No approved agent targets a specific transcript's stability.
HuR/ELAVL1 modulators are preclinical.
routes.applies_when: the transcript is short-lived and the promoter is already active — the case where more transcription achieves nothing
caveats: Entirely invisible to a promoter-level analysis, which is why it is worth checking before concluding the transcriptional route is the only one.
RNA-binding proteins are highly pleiotropic; HuR alone governs hundreds of transcripts.

routes.what_it_does: blocks a microRNA that represses your transcript, raising both message and protein
drugs: No approved antagomir.
Miravirsen and RG-101 (anti-miR-122) reached clinical trials.
routes.applies_when: a specific miRNA is a documented repressor of your gene in your cell type
caveats: One miRNA has hundreds of targets, so this is a low-specificity intervention despite being sequence-directed.
Needs the repressing miRNA identified in the right cell type; a TargetScan prediction is not sufficient evidence.

routes.what_it_does: raises protein output from existing message, usually by relieving a uORF or modulating eIF2-alpha phosphorylation
drugs: No approved agent raises translation of a chosen transcript.
ISRIB and related integrated-stress-response modulators are preclinical.
routes.applies_when: protein is low while transcript is normal — the signature of a translational, not transcriptional, problem
caveats: Global translational modulators move the whole proteome.
An RT-qPCR cannot see this problem OR this solution; you need protein and, ideally, ribosome profiling.

routes.what_it_does: makes the ribosome read through a premature stop codon, so a full-length protein is produced from an allele that otherwise yields a truncated one
drugs: Gentamicin (FDA-approved as an antibiotic; readthrough use is off-label)
Amikacin, tobramycin (same situation)
Ataluren / Translarna (EMA conditional approval for nonsense DMD; the FDA did NOT approve it, and the EMA moved against renewal — do not record this as an approved option)
ELX-02 (clinical, designed to separate readthrough from aminoglycoside toxicity)
routes.applies_when: the gene carries a premature termination codon (PTC)
caveats: Only helps a nonsense allele. A missense, frameshift or deletion allele gets nothing from readthrough.
Aminoglycoside readthrough is weak and the doses implied are nephrotoxic and ototoxic; this is why the class has not become a therapy despite thirty years of interest.
Readthrough inserts a near-cognate amino acid at the stop, so the product is full-length but not necessarily wild-type.
Efficiency depends strongly on the stop codon identity and its sequence context — UGA with a C at +4 reads through best.

routes.what_it_does: stops the surveillance pathway destroying a PTC-bearing transcript, so more message survives to be translated
drugs: No approved NMD inhibitor exists.
SMG1 and UPF1 inhibitors are preclinical.
routes.applies_when: the gene carries a PTC and the transcript is being degraded before translation
caveats: NMD is a general surveillance pathway: blocking it stabilises every PTC-bearing transcript in the cell, not only yours, and roughly a third of normal transcripts are NMD substrates.
Raising a PTC transcript without readthrough gives you more truncated protein, which may be inert or actively harmful. The two mechanisms are usually only interesting together.

post_transcriptional.summary: A promoter-level analysis stops at transcription. These act after it, and for some genes that is where the whole problem is: if the transcript is destroyed or mistranslated, doubling transcription doubles the amount that is destroyed. 1 of 6 mechanism(s) here have an FDA-approved agent. The rest are listed so that an empty transcriptional result is not mistaken for 'nothing can be done' — they are mechanisms, not treatments.

notes: BUB1B is not in the curated redundancy table, which is short and certainly incomplete. Absence here is not evidence that no paralog substitutes — it means nobody has written one down in this file.
compensation.summary: Whether a paralog could substitute for this gene is unanswered. It is worth asking explicitly, because the question 'restore this function' has more answers than 'raise this transcript'.

routes.what_it_does: re-expresses a paralog that was switched off after birth, by interfering with the repressor that closed it
drugs: Hydroxyurea (FDA-approved, sickle cell) — raises HbF
Voxelotor, L-glutamine (approved for sickle cell by other mechanisms; not HbF inducers)
Exagamglogene autotemcel / exa-cel (FDA-approved gene editing that disrupts the BCL11A erythroid enhancer — the switch itself)
Decitabine, azacitidine (approved hypomethylating agents; raise HbF but are cytotoxic)
routes.worked_example: sickle cell disease: HBB is mutated and undruggable, so the intervention raises HBG1/HBG2 instead. The clearest proof that reactivating a silenced paralog beats fixing the broken gene
routes.specificity: comes from the tissue and the repressor, not the drug: BCL11A's erythroid enhancer is lineage-restricted, which is what makes exa-cel targeted rather than global
caveats: Hydroxyurea's HbF mechanism is still incompletely defined after decades of clinical use, and response varies widely between patients.
Hypomethylating agents reactivate the whole methylome, not your locus; they are chemotherapeutics.

routes.what_it_does: re-expresses the silent parental copy of an imprinted gene, leaving the already-expressed copy alone
drugs: Topotecan and other topoisomerase-I inhibitors (FDA-approved in oncology; this use is preclinical repurposing, not an approved indication)
Antisense oligonucleotides against the silencing transcript (clinical for Angelman: rugonersen, ION582, GTX-102)
routes.worked_example: Angelman syndrome: maternal UBE3A is mutated and the paternal copy is imprinted silent. Topoisomerase inhibitors unsilence the paternal allele in mouse models by interfering with the long antisense transcript that represses it
routes.specificity: the ASO route is genuinely sequence-specific. The small-molecule route is not — a topoisomerase inhibitor is a cytotoxic drug and the doses are not plausibly tolerable for a neurological indication
caveats: Only applies to imprinted loci — roughly 150 genes in humans. Check whether yours is one before reading further.
The silent allele must be intact. If both copies carry the mutation, unsilencing achieves nothing.
Most of the mouse data is developmental; the window in which reactivation helps may close.

routes.what_it_does: re-expresses the gene from the inactive X in a heterozygous female, where roughly half of cells silence the healthy copy
drugs: No approved agent.
XIST-directed ASOs and combined DNMT/EZH2 inhibition are preclinical.
routes.worked_example: Rett syndrome: MECP2 is X-linked, and in heterozygous females the wild-type copy sits on the inactive X in half of neurons. Reactivating it would be curative in those cells
routes.specificity: essentially none at present. X-reactivation is genome-scale by definition, and reactivating the whole inactive X risks overexpressing hundreds of genes
caveats: Only relevant for X-linked genes in heterozygous females.
MECP2 in particular is dose-sensitive in both directions — duplication causes its own syndrome, so overshooting is harmful rather than merely wasteful.

routes.what_it_does: removes the methylation holding a CpG-island promoter shut, so the existing machinery can transcribe it again
drugs: Azacitidine, decitabine (FDA-approved, MDS/AML)
Cedazuridine/decitabine (approved oral combination)
routes.worked_example: tumour-suppressor reactivation in myelodysplastic syndrome, where the therapeutic effect is attributed partly to re-expressing methylation-silenced genes
routes.specificity: none at the locus level. These reactivate every methylation-silenced promoter in the genome, which is why they are useful in malignancy and hard to justify otherwise
caveats: Myelosuppressive, and the global reactivation includes retroelements and genes you did not want.
Only works if your promoter is actually methylated — worth measuring before assuming, and this package does not look at methylation at all.

Already represented in the chromatin-level category, where its specificity is scored at ~0.05. Listed here because the *reason* to use it is different: a specific silenced allele, not a general nudge.

notes: BUB1B is not in the curated imprinted or developmental-switch lists, which are short. That is not evidence the gene is unsilenced — **nothing in this package measures methylation, imprinting or allele-specific expression.** If your gene is silenced rather than merely low, every transcriptional route above is aimed at the wrong problem, and the way to find out is allele-specific RT-qPCR or bisulphite sequencing.
reactivation.summary: Whether this gene is silenced rather than merely low is unmeasured here, and it changes which routes make sense. Allele-specific expression is the experiment that settles it.

degradation.degron: a KEN box and a D-box
degradation.when: at mitotic exit, once the checkpoint is satisfied
degradation.protected_by: acetylation of the protein is reported to block its recognition by Cdc20, so the balance - not the ligase alone - sets the level. Verify in the primary literature before building on it; this is a pointer, not a result of this run.
degradation.note: BUBR1 is a checkpoint protein that the checkpoint's own target complex destroys, so its level is tied to the cycle it controls. Blocking that destruction also blocks mitotic exit, which is why this route is harder than it looks for a gene of this kind.

routes.what_it_does: blocks the 26S proteasome, so ubiquitinated proteins are not destroyed and levels rise
drugs: Bortezomib (FDA-approved, myeloma)
Carfilzomib (FDA-approved)
Ixazomib (FDA-approved, oral)
routes.specificity_note: essentially none: the proteasome degrades most of the proteome, so this raises thousands of proteins at once
caveats: These are cytotoxic oncology drugs with neuropathy and cardiotoxicity. Using one to raise a single protein is not a plausible therapy outside malignancy.
Useful mainly as an EXPERIMENT: if your protein rises under proteasome inhibition, degradation is the limiting step and transcriptional routes are aimed at the wrong place.

routes.what_it_does: prevents lysosomal degradation, raising proteins cleared by autophagy rather than the proteasome
drugs: Hydroxychloroquine (FDA-approved)
Chloroquine (FDA-approved)
routes.specificity_note: non-specific, and the two degradation routes are distinct - which one clears your protein decides which drug could matter
caveats: Retinal toxicity limits chronic dosing.
Equally a diagnostic: it tells you which degradation pathway your protein uses.

routes.what_it_does: binds a misfolding-prone protein and stabilises a foldable conformation, so it escapes quality control and traffics normally
drugs: Migalastat (FDA-approved, Fabry disease - stabilises mutant alpha-galactosidase A)
Tafamidis (FDA-approved, ATTR - stabilises the transthyretin tetramer)
Acoramidis (FDA-approved, ATTR)
Lumacaftor, tezacaftor, elexacaftor (FDA-approved, CF - correctors that stabilise mutant CFTR folding)
routes.specificity_note: genuinely high: a chaperone binds one protein, and this is the only route in this section with real selectivity
caveats: Needs a specific misfolding mutation with residual function. Migalastat works only for amenable GLA variants - roughly a third of patients - and does nothing for a null allele.
No chaperone exists unless someone has developed one for your protein specifically; this is a discovery programme, not a route you can take today.

routes.what_it_does: blocks the specific ligase that ubiquitinates your protein, so only your protein accumulates
drugs: No approved inhibitor of a named E3 for this purpose.
MDM2 inhibitors (idasanutlin, navtemadlin) are the closest clinical example, raising p53.
routes.specificity_note: potentially high - an E3 has a limited substrate set - but it requires knowing which ligase degrades your protein
caveats: The limiting knowledge is the ligase-substrate pair. For most proteins nobody has identified it.
This is the mirror image of a PROTAC: the same biology used to raise rather than destroy.

notes: These leave transcription alone. If your protein is made normally and degraded too fast, every transcriptional route in this report is aimed at the wrong step - and nothing in this package can tell the two apart.
The experiment that distinguishes them: compare transcript and protein. Normal mRNA with low protein points here; low mRNA points at everything above.

Specificity is the problem for three of these four. A proteasome inhibitor raises most of the proteome, which makes it an excellent diagnostic and a poor therapy. The pharmacological chaperone is the exception, and it needs a chaperone to exist for your protein.
